newsitem.title: CHINA: China's top HK general dines on U.S. Navy flagship.
newsitem.headline: China's top HK general dines on U.S. Navy flagship.

text.p: China's top general in Hong Kong lunched with an American admiral on Wednesday during the U.S. Navy's first port call since China took over the former British colony last month, officials said.

The commander of the Seventh Fleet, Vice Admiral Bob Natter, also paid a courtesy call on the People's Liberation Army (PLA) garrison chiefs at their headquarters, still named the Prince of Wales Barracks, the officials said.
Natter's group was the first foreign visitors to the tightly sealed base since the PLA moved in on July 1.
After a two-hour lunch aboard the flagship USS Blue Ridge, Natter described his meeting with garrison commander Lieutenant-General Liu Zhenwu as cordial.
The Blue Ridge, which began a five-day stay on Monday, is the first foreign warship to visit Hong Kong since it reverted to Chinese rule on July 1, ending more than 150 years of British rule.
"The closer we could work with the PLA, I think, it will be better off for everyone," Natter told reporters.
"We want to engage with the Chinese leadership. I think it is very clear from the leadership of our country."
"That's certainly my effort and my intention here, so that if problems happen to arise in the future, we can deal with them quickly and efficiently," he said.
Officers said Liu was impressed with the Blue Ridge when he toured the ship, which is on a regular port visit for recreation and supplies along with the USS Guardian and Patriot anti-mine ships.
The U.S. Navy makes 60 to 70 port visit to Hong Kong a year, bringing US$50 million into the local economy.
Beijing and Washington reached agreement in April allowing the U.S. to continue Hong Kong port visits after the handover.
Many people in Hong Kong view the PLA with alarm because of its role in the bloody 1989 crackdown of a student-led democracy protest in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
A Chinese diplomat told Reuters the PLA had tried to keep a low profile so far because of unfriendly press coverage and that it was going through a learning process in public relations.
